title: Own-authority truckload freight brokerage for small/mid Midwest shippers (dry van)
product_service: Arranging full-truckload dry-van moves for shippers using vetted third-party carriers; quoting, tendering, tracking, billing, claims handling.
target_customer: Logistics/shipping managers or owners at small-to-mid manufacturers, distributors and CPG/packaging companies ($5M-$300M revenue) without large-broker attention; Midwest origin lanes.
purchase_motivation: Need reliable capacity on short notice, spot coverage when contract carriers reject, price, service responsiveness.
spending_evidence: Very large existing spend: C.H. Robinson NAST alone billed $3.83B in Q3 2026 [A, WS07-S008]; RXO brokerage $1.43B in Q3 2026 [A, WS07-S010]; FMCSA estimate implies ~33,000 registered brokers in 2022 [A-derived, WS07-S001].
representative_operators: C.H. Robinson — NAST revenue $3.83B Q3 2026, AGP ~13.5% of revenue [A, WS07-S008]
RXO — brokerage GM 12.6% Q3 2026; being acquired by CHR ($5.8B) [A, WS07-S010]
Landstar — agent model, purchased transportation 78.2% of revenue [A, WS07-S011]
TQL, Echo, Arrive, Uber Freight — large privately held/private-equity peers (sizes not verified)
revenue_mechanism: Spread between shipper rate and carrier pay per load (gross margin), plus accessorials.
typical_transaction_value: Incumbent truck revenue ~$2,811/load (Landstar Q3 2026) [A, WS07-S011]; incumbent AGP ~13.5% => ~$300-$400 gross per load [A-derived, WS07-S008]; new entrant spot loads 10-20% margin [E].
direct_costs: Carrier linehaul pay (82-90% of revenue), load-board/TMS subscriptions, carrier-vetting tools, factoring/quick-pay cost, cargo-claim deductibles, bad debt.
contribution_profit_note: ~$250-$400 gross per load at 12-15% on ~$2,500 loads [E, anchored on A comps]; after factoring (~2%/30 days of invoice, WS07-S017 D) and tools, ~$180-$330 contribution per load [E].
working_capital_note: Structural negative: incumbent CHR carries ~61 days of receivables vs ~39 days payables [A-derived, WS07-S009]; shippers pay 30-60+ days while small carriers expect quick pay [D, WS07-S017]. At $250k/month revenue a new broker funds roughly $150k-$250k of carrier pay or pays ~1-5%/30 days to a factor [E]. BMC-85 route ties up $75k cash/ILOC [A, WS07-S001]; BMC-84 route depends on personal credit for premium/collateral [E].
sales_cycle: Spot quotes same-day; becoming a routing-guide/backup carrier 1-6 months; primary contract lanes require RFP cycles (annual).
repeat_purchase: recurring — shippers tender weekly/daily once a broker is in the routing guide
customer_accessibility: Shippers are identifiable (manufacturer databases, import records) and reachable by phone; but they are bombarded by broker cold calls and credibility/track record gates primary freight.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed abundant carrier supply via load boards historically (>70,000 capacity providers at Landstar alone [A, WS07-S012]), but capacity tightened in 2026 as non-domiciled/ELP enforcement removed drivers [C, WS07-S014, WS07-S015].
competitive_intensity: extreme — tens of thousands of brokers, consolidation (CHR acquiring RXO), AI-enabled incumbents cutting headcount (NAST -11.4% YoY) [A, WS07-S008].
entry_strategy: Lane-density focus (e.g., a few Chicago-outbound corridors) and 24/7 responsiveness for shippers too small for large-broker account teams; start as agent (WS07-002) to build book before own authority.
licenses: FMCSA property-broker operating authority via Motus (identity proofing; min. 8 business days review) [A, WS07-S002]; OP-1 filing fee reportedly $300 [D, WS07-S005]; $75,000 financial security on BMC-84 surety bond or BMC-85 trust limited since 2026-01-16 to cash/ILOC/Treasuries [A, WS07-S001]; BOC-3 process agent filing [A, WS07-S002]; UCR $46 (2026) rising to $55 (2027) [A, WS07-S003, WS07-S004]; contingent cargo + general liability insurance not federally mandated but shippers usually require it [E]; no Illinois property-broker license identified [E, not verified].
regulatory_barriers: Immediate-suspension rule: if bond/trust drawn below $75k and not replenished within 7 calendar days of FMCSA notice, authority is suspended [A, WS07-S001]; broker-transparency (371.3) supplemental proposal pending at OIRA [C, WS07-S007]; negligent-selection liability exposure (case law, not reviewed) [E].
operational_risks: Double-brokering, fictitious pickups and identity-theft carriers; cargo-theft losses ~$725M in 2025 (+60%) with schemes using acquired carriers [C, WS07-S016]; service failures on tight-capacity days.
financial_risks: Shipper insolvency/bad debt; margin squeeze when contracted sell rates lag carrier cost (CHR cost/mile +33.5% vs rate +31.5%) [A, WS07-S008]; bond drawdown from unpaid carrier claims; factoring recourse.
geographic_constraints: None legally; Chicago lanes give density; can serve nationally by phone.
founder_expertise: Freight pricing, lane knowledge, carrier vetting/fraud screening, credit control, TMS use; selling to shipping managers.
staffing: Founder sells and books initially; first hire carrier sales/ops rep at ~$40-60k + commission once ~5-10 loads/day [E].
automation_potential: Rate quoting from benchmarks, carrier outreach/email parsing, track-and-trace updates, document/invoice matching, carrier identity screening — real but incumbents (CHR AI agents) already deploy it.
delegation_potential: Moderate-high: broker reps are a standard labor market; book-of-business key-person risk remains.
scalability: Add reps and lanes; mature small brokerages run many desks; ceiling large but returns decline as competition grows.
expansion: LTL, reefer, flatbed, drayage, managed transportation, warehousing partners, freight audit.
roic_note: Asset-light but working-capital-heavy; if $50-100k is at risk (bond collateral + WC) and op profit ~$100k, ROIC ~100-200% [E]; factoring lowers capital but takes ~10-15% of gross margin [E].
critical_assumptions: New entrant can achieve 12-18% margins on mostly spot/transactional freight
Founder can win 3-10 shipper accounts in year 1 by cold outreach
Founder personal credit qualifies for affordable BMC-84 bond (else $75k BMC-85)
Fraud losses can be kept below ~1% of revenue with vetting tools
unanswered_questions: Primary-source confirmation of the $300 OP-1 fee (FMCSA site blocked)
Census SUSB firm-size distribution for NAICS 488510 (not retrieved)
Current BMC-84 premium ranges by credit tier
Survival rate of new broker authorities after 2-3 years
failure_modes: Never gets past spot quoting into routing guides
One shipper default wipes out a year of margin
Double-brokered/stolen load leads to claim and bond drawdown
Rate spikes squeeze committed sell rates
Founder cannot hire reps who retain books
score_rationale: fcf 5: $100k-ish base yr-3 plausible, upside exists; entry 3: extreme crowding and consolidation; cash 3: negative cash cycle documented at incumbents; resilience 4: 2022-25 freight recession and 2026 spike show high cyclicality; ai 6: real productivity gains but incumbents have them too.
preliminary_verdict: advance — huge, liquid market with documented incumbent margins; viable only with lane-density wedge, strict fraud/credit controls and probably an agent phase first.

title: Independent freight agent under a host brokerage (agent-to-agency path)
subindustry: Freight agent / agency under host broker authority
product_service: Selling and managing truckload freight for shippers under a host broker's MC authority, bond, insurance, credit, carrier vetting and back office; agent keeps a split of gross margin.
target_customer: Same SMB shippers as WS07-001; host brokerages recruiting agents.
purchase_motivation: Shippers: capacity and service. Host broker: agents bring books of business without salary cost.
spending_evidence: Landstar pays agents 7.8% of revenue ($117.7M in Q3 2026) [A, WS07-S011]; 457 Landstar 'Million Dollar Agents' produce 95% of revenue [A, WS07-S012].
representative_operators: Landstar — ~960 independent commission sales agents [A, WS07-S012]
Numerous agent-model brokers (e.g., Trinity Logistics, Allen Lund agent programs — not verified)
revenue_mechanism: Commission = agreed split (commonly 60-80% to agent) of load gross margin [D, WS07-S018], or % of revenue (Landstar avg 7.8%) [A, WS07-S011].
typical_transaction_value: Load ~$2,800 revenue [A, WS07-S011]; gross ~$300-$400; agent share ~$180-$300 per load at 60-70% split [D/E].
direct_costs: Agent's own phone/software/marketing; sometimes desk fees, chargebacks for bad debt or claims per contract [D].
contribution_profit_note: At $1M annual agent revenue and Landstar-like 7.8% of revenue, ~$78k gross commission before agent's own costs [A-derived, WS07-S011]; at $3M, ~$235k [E].
working_capital_note: Host pays carriers and carries receivables/credit risk (Landstar operating subsidiaries contract with customers and assume credit risk [A, WS07-S012]); agent usually paid after shipper pays [E]. Near-zero working capital.
sales_cycle: Same as brokerage: spot quotes days; routing-guide inclusion 1-6 months.
repeat_purchase: recurring — tendered freight from routing-guide shippers
customer_accessibility: As WS07-001 but host's credit, insurance certificates and track record remove part of the credibility wall.
supplier_accessibility: Host provides vetted carrier network and tools [D, WS07-S018].
competitive_intensity: high — agent recruiting is competitive; splits vary; shippers already have many brokers.
entry_strategy: Low-cost validation of whether the founder can sell freight before committing $75k bond and WC; specialise in a lane/vertical; negotiate contract preserving customer ownership/non-solicit terms to allow later conversion to own authority.
licenses: None for agent personally (operates under host authority); host must hold broker authority + $75k security [A, WS07-S001]; agent contract terms (non-compete/non-solicit) [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low. Must avoid acting as unregistered broker outside host relationship (FMCSA broker/bona fide agent guidance) [A, WS07-S006].
operational_risks: Host instability or slow carrier pay damages agent reputation [D, WS07-S018]; fraud still possible but host vetting helps.
financial_risks: Chargebacks for bad debt/claims if contract assigns them; host insolvency could freeze commissions.
founder_expertise: Freight sales and operations; host training partially covers it.
staffing: Solo initially; later sub-agents or assistants paid from commission.
automation_potential: Prospecting, quote prep, tracking emails; host TMS.
delegation_potential: Low-moderate: book lives with the agent; can build an agency office with reps (Landstar's larger agents run multi-person offices) [E].
scalability: Capped by split; real scaling usually means converting to own authority or building a multi-rep agency.
expansion: Convert to own authority (WS07-001) once book exceeds ~$2-3M revenue [E]; add verticals.
roic_note: Capital at risk <$5k; any profit gives ROIC >1,000% — but return is mostly on founder labor.
critical_assumptions: A reputable host will sign an unproven agent with fair split and no punitive non-compete
Founder can generate ~$1M+ annual freight revenue within 18-24 months
Agent is not saddled with bad-debt chargebacks
unanswered_questions: Typical non-solicit/book-ownership terms in agent contracts
Distribution of agent revenue (median, not just Million Dollar Agents)
Survival rate of new agents in first 24 months
failure_modes: Agent cannot build book and quits
Split erodes economics vs own authority
score_rationale: roic 8 / cash 8: host funds carriers and credit [A]; delegation 3 and scale 4: mostly founder book; fcf 4: commission ceiling unless converted.
preliminary_verdict: advance — cheapest, fastest way to test whether the founder can sell freight (hundreds of dollars), with a documented conversion path to WS07-001.

title: Temperature-controlled (reefer) brokerage for Chicago-area food & beverage manufacturers

representative_operators: C.H. Robinson (large reefer/produce franchise; segment size not broken out) [A, WS07-S008]
Many specialized reefer brokers (names/sizes not verified)
revenue_mechanism: Load spread; temperature-controlled loads typically command higher per-load revenue [E].
typical_transaction_value: ~$3,000-$4,000 per long-haul reefer load at Oct-2026 rates [E from WS07-S013 per-mile data]; 10-16% margin [E].
direct_costs: Reefer carrier pay, higher-limit cargo insurance, claims deductibles, factoring.
contribution_profit_note: ~$300-$500 per load gross [E]; one rejected/spoiled load can cost several loads' margin [E].
working_capital_note: Same negative cycle as WS07-001 [A-derived, WS07-S009]; claims can tie up cash for months [E].
sales_cycle: Spot same-day; food shippers run annual RFPs; seasonal (produce) bid cycles.
repeat_purchase: recurring — daily/weekly outbound to retailer DCs
acquisition_channels: Outreach to food manufacturers and co-packers
customer_accessibility: Food manufacturers are identifiable (FDA facility registration not public in detail; trade directories) [E]; credibility wall high due to spoilage risk.
supplier_accessibility: Reefer capacity tighter than van; spot nearly equals contract (spread $0.02/mi) [C, WS07-S013], so carriers have leverage.
competitive_intensity: high — produce/reefer is a classic broker vertical.
entry_strategy: Focus on Chicago food corridor outbound lanes, temperature-monitoring documentation, claims discipline.
licenses: FMCSA property-broker operating authority via Motus (identity proofing; min. 8 business days review) [A, WS07-S002]; OP-1 filing fee reportedly $300 [D, WS07-S005]; $75,000 financial security on BMC-84 surety bond or BMC-85 trust limited since 2026-01-16 to cash/ILOC/Treasuries [A, WS07-S001]; BOC-3 process agent filing [A, WS07-S002]; UCR $46 (2026) rising to $55 (2027) [A, WS07-S003, WS07-S004]; contingent cargo + general liability insurance not federally mandated but shippers usually require it [E]; no Illinois property-broker license identified [E, not verified]. FDA Sanitary Transportation rule (21 CFR Part 1 Subpart O) duties may apply to brokers acting as 'shippers' [E, not verified].
regulatory_barriers: Food-safety transport compliance; same FMCSA broker rules.
operational_risks: Temperature excursions, rejected loads, food & beverage is a frequent cargo-theft target [E; CargoNet commodity breakdown not retrieved].
financial_risks: Large claims (whole load value), shipper concentration, contract-rate squeeze when spot≈contract [C, WS07-S013].
geographic_constraints: Chicago-area food cluster gives density; not required.
founder_expertise: Reefer operations (pulp temps, continuous vs cycle, pre-cooling), claims handling, food-safety paperwork.
automation_potential: Telematics temperature feeds, automated exception alerts, quoting.
delegation_potential: Moderate; reefer desk skills are hireable.
scalability: Add reps and lanes; food demand resilient.
expansion: Cold-storage partnerships, LTL reefer consolidation, produce seasonality desks.
roic_note: Similar to WS07-001 with higher claim risk capital buffer [E].
critical_assumptions: Food shippers accept a new broker for backup/spot lanes
Claims kept below ~1% of revenue
unanswered_questions: Chicago-area food manufacturing establishment counts (Census CBP not retrieved)
Typical reefer broker margins vs van (no public split)
FSMA sanitary-transport obligations for brokers
failure_modes: Tight reefer capacity forces negative-margin coverage
RFP-dominated buyers never award a newcomer
score_rationale: resilience 6: food demand less cyclical; access 4: spoilage risk makes shippers conservative; cash 3: negative cycle plus claims.
preliminary_verdict: hold — defensible vertical with resilient demand, but higher claim risk and weaker access than general van; best as a second desk after WS07-001/002.

staffing: Founder + carrier reps; experienced flatbed reps command premium.

Count of steel service centers/building-material distributors in Chicago region

representative_operators: C.H. Robinson (largest LTL 3PL; LTL AGP +8%) [A, WS07-S008]
RXO [A, WS07-S010]
Freightquote/Freightcenter-type online LTL brokers (not verified)

Markups of 15%+ survive comparison shopping

Terms for small 3PL carrier agreements with national LTL carriers
